title: The Arcadia Ballroom tryout: the boss asks the band to play softly like Autrey
summary: Joining Charlie Johnson's band at the Arcadia, his soft open-horn playing of 'Cocktails for Two' impressed the owner, Mr. Corrigan, who asked the others to sound like him.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Well, before that -- I'm kind of proud of that idea, of that guy saying Herman Autrey, used a mute like Herman? Well, a few things happened in my life, concerning the mute. When I was working with Charlie Johnson's band at the -- 53rd and Broadway there, the Arcadia Ballroom.

That was -- well, I started to say, a hard place to play in -- excuse me. It was hard to play in because they did not want you to blast and hurt the people's ears, but you know, that was -- with all these mirrors turning around the ballroom there, you know, the notes would bounce off, and then kill you. So I didn't have that trouble. So I was one of the new guys that Charlie hired, and I went in to -- in the -- tried to do -- said well come up, we'll give you a try out, and see how you sound, so I'll never forget it. Bah dah dah deedle dee dah dee, this was the tune I had to play. Nuh, nuh, nuh, nuh, nuh, nuh, deedle dee dee dah -- Listening --

Cocktails, so I went in and I played it, and I noticed the boss would come, Mr. Corrigan was his name. I'll never forget him. And after I played that for a while they seemed to like my playing, and let's see, they had Jack Butter Buckley playing trumpet. They had -- what's his name, he used to play with Fletcher -- who used to, Garvin Bushell on sax. Let's see. Emmett Matthews on tenor sax. I should be able to (Unintelligible) name the whole band, because I worked with them for quite a while.

But he came down, and he said Charlie, soften the band down. He said, and besides, why can't those -- your other trumpet player's there, play like this new fellow? He said, and this new fellow -- he said what they call those

things they stick in the -- in the horn? He say mutes, a mute. He said well I don't -- I notice he doesn't use one, but why don't they sound like him when he plays? You know, because I didn't blast and at that time I wasn't missing many notes, baby.
Those things seemed to help a lot, you know, when you play.
But you were playing open horn, soft open horn.

Yeah, open horn off and on, you know. And (unintelligible) and in those days the arrangements called for straight -- well, the parts were marked, straight mute, harmony mute, cupped mute, they had to have -- and derby hat, you know. In other words you have to go -- all three horns, three trumpet players change at the same time, and to get the sound that the arrangement called for, you know?
